While walking along the bike path we noticed a small, buffy sparrow with big head and a short tail scurry behind a bush near (37.4355120, -122.0923952). It was secretive in behavior…it would scurry or take low long hops between bushes then stand perfectly still. Crouched stance most of the time and very quiet. Large head and large bill, with a gently slope that made a smooth ongoing line (seemingly no angle between bill and forehead). Fairly plain face with thin brown streak behind the eye, dark brown crown with pale center stripe, and pale complete eye ring. Intricate pattern on back/wings with reddish spots in center of each feather, edged with black. Seemed like it had a short yellow eyebrow/streak above the front of the eye. Pale-orange/buffy face and belly. No streaking on belly/chest, but some faint buffy streaks near armpit and lower back flank. By the time we tried to get pictures through our binoculars it was on the move, heading under another bush and then flew low across the pave path to the steep hillside next to the salt pond…we lost it. I have a few blurry pictures, unfortunately not great. BUT SO EXCITING!!! This is the first grasshopper sparrow we have had in the county. We weren’t even paying attention to birds in the field…just awesome luck to see an odd shaped sparrow dart under a bush.

While sorting through a flock in alders on the north side of the bridge, I noticed a large flycatcher pop up onto the wires that run just above the riparian on the south side of the bridge. I could see that it looked bright yellow below, but my momentary expectation that it would be a Tropical Kingbird was dispelled immediately as I got bins on it and saw a large Myiarchus with a bright yellow belly looking back at me. Instantly the hand-shaking adrenaline rush and the get-photos reflex were triggered, and after securing photos I ran to a better vantage with respect to lighting where I could also see the bird's back well enough to get an idea of the tertial pattern. A minute later the bird dropped down from the wire into the alders, and I made calls and so on to get the word out. I stayed until dusk with a large group of observers and, unfortunately, we were all unable to relocate the bird, although some thought they might have heard calls around sunset.

The bright and saturated rich lemon-yellow color of the belly was immediately obvious, so much so that (again) it was momentarily suggestive of Tropical Kingbird. Also immediately obvious were the very large size and, in particular, the rather large bill. Even in my first views, the large pale pinkish-yellowish zone at the base of the bill and the darkish gray upper chest and throat, contrasting sharply with the yellow lower chest and belly but not contrasting strongly with the remainder of the dark brownish head, were apparent too. In better lighting, these features were still apparent, in fact more obvious, and it was also possible to see crisp white lines at the top of the wing panel formed by white outer webs to the tertials. Although my views were not optimal for assessing the cleanness of these white markings, nor the exact extents of the white in each feather, I thought that the uppermost of these white lines appeared thicker and shorter than the lower 1–2. That is consistent with the tertial pattern expected in GCFL, with a nearly fully white outer web to the innermost (i.e., in the folded wing, uppermost) tertial. The wingbars were distinctly buff-tinged. The face, auriculars, crown, and remainder of the head were brownish and barely (if at all) darker than the throat, not contrastingly strongly with the throat. The tail was rather long, but so were the wings, making the tail not appear terribly long in proportion. I was unable to resolve details of rectrix pattern other than noting that the underside of the tail appeared uniformly rufous from a distance. 

The saturated yellow underparts, fairly sharp transition to the gray chest, dark tone of the gray chest and throat, minimal contrast between the color of the throat and that of the rest of the head, large bill with extensive pale zone at the base, and very bulky appearance are inconsistent with Ash-throated; while views of the tertials were not optimal, they still suggested the extensive white in the innermost tertial characteristic of GCFL and also inconsistent with Ash-throated. The saturation of the yellow below, the strong contrast with the fairly dark gray chest, the darkish throat, and the bill (being large but not massive and with an extensive pale base to the lower mandible) are suggestive of GCFL over Brown-crested. Photographs support all these features except for tertial pattern (tertials not visible in photos). It is worth noting that in the field this bird appeared still more richly colored below than the photos suggest.

A fairly cooperative bird working the willows south of the barn, first at (37.1315392, -122.3129582) and then later relocated with other observers at various spots in the willow patch. Initially detected by its scold, with short repeated nasal "rehr rehr rehr" calls each with a rising-then-falling cadence, unlike the scold of any common vireo. I am familiar with this scold and knew to look for a Philly Vireo immediately upon hearing it, but all I could see at first were two Hutton's, which was puzzling—the scold really sounded like a Philly and not like any Hutton's I have ever heard—and then the Philly popped out in front of me and provided good views as I followed it for the next fifteen minutes, and again when refound more than an hour later. It was rather slow-moving and sat still for periods, which explained why I struggled to see it at first; it was presumably sitting still somewhere obscured by vegetation. This was a moderately bright individual with a strong yellow wash to the underparts, clearly strongest on the throat and the upper part of the chest, becoming weaker toward the belly and flanks; a strongly patterned face with dark lores and a bold transocular, a rather short supercilium, a short and fairly stout bill, and a round head, all imparting a cute and somewhat feisty/spunky-looking facial expression, unlike the pale lores and blank face of WAVI; shorter tail and stockier build than WAVI; and distinctive scold, unlike the long slow dragged-out rasping scold calls of WAVI. This is a very late date, with only a handful (c. 3?) later records for NorCal. Within a mile of the Cascade Ck Bell's Vireo spot and within a quarter-mile of the Pie Ranch Blue-headed Vireo spot! First heard calling 30 feet north of the trail at: (37.8673771, -122.3102690), making squeaky Song Sparrow like bark calls, with single barks at first, followed by often double or triple barks. The bird later also gave the typical WIWR chatter call, similar to the recording in the Sibley app. The bird then came close, first giving good views in the willow clump on the north side of the trail at (37.8671807, -122.3103444), then crossing to the willow thicket at the southeast corner of the intersection of the main trail and the small spur trail (in the same spot where I found the first county record in 2024). Eventually moved south to (37.8664338, -122.3103592), before popping up again near the original location on the north side of the main trail. Last heard at 8:40am at about (37.8672398, -122.3105439). Pale overall, with a distinctly whitish throat and textured pale coloration extending across the entire side of the face, including the auriculars. The whitish pebbled/scaled texture extended downward from the throat, through the lower breast and upper flanks. The lower flanks were barred with dark blackish interspersed with thin white bands. Whitish supercilium, with a medium brown line extending rearward from the eye. The medium brown crown and nape merged with a brown to chestnut back and a short chestnut tail with dark barring. Tiny white spangles on the lesser and median wing coverts, brown and buff barring on the primaries. When brightly lit, the upper parts appeared almost rufous in color. This is purely speculative, but given that this bird was observed in the same location (sometimes perching in nearly identical spots in the same willows), this could be the same returning individual that I found in November, 2024 and which continued through March 2025. Interestingly, that bird had a distinctive depigmented (mostly white) left alula. Unfortunately, my photos didn't capture that feature well on the current bird. The 2024 bird was later accepted by CBRC ( a first record for the county), but was not detected in the winter of 2025/2026. See https://ebird.org/checklist/S203502632 for the 2024 observation. BCC!!!!!!!! Unbelievably electric to see an exquisite Mexican pine-loving mountain microwarbler in riparian at Pescadero Marsh. A stunning bird at (37.2577725, -122.3950345), in an arroyo willow when I found it at about 1:30 pm. It was initially quite cooperative and allowed a couple minutes of excellent views and reasonably good photos. I lost the bird while getting word out, but it was refound and seen briefly by Chris Hayward, Malia DeFelice, and others high in pines at the same location about an hour later, and then refound again by Cédric Duhalde and seen by many others later in the day, after I had to leave. 

This is a first for San Mateo County and is the c. 8th record for NorCal (excluding records from the mountains of Tulare and Mono), following two from Monterey, two from Santa Cruz, two from SF (one of them being from SEFI), and one from Mendocino. Of these, three (1 MTY, 1 SF, 1 MEN) wintered or attempted to winter; the remaining four were fall migrants, spanning the dates 9/6 (a one-day MTY migrant) to 10/15 (the second day of the two-day stay of the migrant record from SEFI). The wintering SF bird returned on 9/19 last year. Continuing second state record. About 11a.m. on 22 Oct., Marty Freeland found a Yellow-browed Warbler in Moss Beach. I went as soon as I could, which was about 24 hours later, arriving shortly before 3p.m. on Oct. 23rd. To describe the location briefly, at this location there is a small, rectangular, dirt parking lot, bounded on the southeast and southwest sides by willows. There is a small bridge through the willows that connects the parking lot to a paddock or sand school just southeast of the parking lot. The sand school is bounded on the north edge by the same clump of willows; maybe 200 feet of them. At about 3:30, I heard the surprisingly loud call of the Yellow-browed Warbler from the willows near the bridge.About 20 people congregated, but we did not see the bird, so I walked around to the other side of that willow clump to look, where Paul Saraceni had been standing since my arrival. Soon after walking up next to Paul (who if I remember correctly, had also heard the bird call), he exclaimed that he had the bird and quickly put me on it. Thank you, Paul! The bird was fairly frantic, with a similar activity level to a kinglet, and remained in the highest shady branches of the willows for about 5 minutes. Thus it allowed me a number of very brief views. It then flew southwestward, and was soon relocated when only a couple minutes later called loudly three times in rapid succession. I then got two nice—but fleeting—looks of it on a sunny willow branch, before it flew off north and I left a bit after 4:00. 
	The call was a shockingly loud, thin call. It fell in pitch at the start and rose towards the end, and was reminiscent of the “suweep!” of a Western Flycatcher. Visually, this was a small, kinglet-sized bird that appeared overall a dull green or pale gray. To me it appeared greenish above and pale below, with a short and stubby bill. It had a bold and prominent pale supercilium that extended from the lores back well behind the eye, a palish wingbar (I was told there were two, but my views only sufficient to see one), and perhaps a paler and slightly contrasting throat. I have seen very few Phylloscopus sp. in my life; including Dusky, Willow, and Wood. If I were to compare this bird to a Wood Warbler, I would describe it as duller green overall; shorter billed and winged, i.e., closer to the shape of a kinglet; and with a wingbar. That is all I was able to gather visually. Obviously, the call is distinctive.

Outstanding find by Marty Freeland! A small, grayish-green, kinglet-like warbler with a small bill with some yellow, a long, pale, high-contrast supercilium, and two wing bars. It gave occasional high-pitched “suweet” calls as it foraged frantically deep in the willows, making looping flycatching sallies. Possibly the worst photos of the m.ob.

LFM notes: astoundingly small and fast-moving, even more so than RCKI. While superficially kinglet-like, this bird stood out as more "long" than "round", with paler underparts, and an obvious pale eyebrow, mostly white and maybe slightly yellow toward forehead. Upperparts had some distinct greenish yellow, and also showed a dark "kinglet bar" behind the second white wingbar. In certain binocular views at certain angles, the auricular appeared somewhat stippled and the pale throat looked lightly streaked with dark gray. Lower mandible of bill about 2/3s pale orange at the base. Legs pale. Foraging behavior frantic, rarely sitting still for more than a couple seconds. Often would drop and do a looping flycatching maneuver, circling quickly back up to the spot it left. Calls heard were a joyous, whistled "su-weet!" slightly reminiscent of Western Flycatcher, sometimes while foraging but definitely the few times it flew between willow patches.

The presence of two wingbars eliminates many Phylloscopus. The possible similar species would be Two-barred (would show longer tail, larger more obvious orangey bill, and would lack "kinglet bar"), Hume's Leaf-Warbler (would be duller, with darker bill and legs), and Pallas's Leaf-Warbler (would have much bolder head pattern with median crown stripe, and smaller bill). The call heard numerous times also helps eliminate many other possible species.

Small-to-medium Phylloscopus warbler with broad, creamy eyeline and wing bars (two) to match. Small, orange-based bill; gray crown without obvious median stripe; crisp, sooty line through eye. Upper back olive-brown; primaries and lower back with a hint of yellow. Flanks and belly creamy-gray, perhaps with a very light yellow cast (though it was tough to see with the bird backlit, against the sky for much of my vigil). Tail gray and without any white. The wing bars rule out Dusky, Arctic, and Kamchatka Leaf Warblers; Pallas's Leaf Warbler is smaller with yellow lines on head/face an an obvious pale rump.  A quick, upsweeping two syllable 'suwee' call, given at long intervals, eliminated Hume's and Two-barred. Bay Area bike bird #376. San Mateo County bike bird #310. An amazing experience with a moderately dull bird, initially at (37.7702658, -122.4763537). It then worked east along the lakeshore halfway to the concrete bridge before flying north across the street to the thick stuff at the top of the Log Cabin Trail hill, where I lost it. It was then not seen until Dario refound it at sunset back in the lakeside willows, which I would imagine are the best place to look. It was giving a loud, sweet, slightly breathy chip, kind of like a weaker California Towhee, intermediate in quality between Hooded and Orange-crowned warblers. 

A very large warbler, mainly rich saturated yellow in color with a white crissum and slate-blue wings and tail, duller yellow on the face and above grading into greenish-yellow on the back, large eye and bill on otherwise blank face (maybe slightly dusky lores?), a rather blank facial expression, striking undertail pattern slightly reminiscent of Magnolia, mainly white from the underside with black tips/edges, forming an interesting pattern when spread. Very little white visible from above, suggesting HY (in combination with its also being rather dull), but views and photos did not permit seeing whether white was limited to the three outermost rectrices or not. Cooperative when in lakeside willows and rather slow-moving. I first saw its face staring me down, and seeing the bright yellow face of a medium, large-billed, blank-faced passerine, it looked almost like an Orchard Oriole. And then a microsecond later it looked obviously like a Prothonotary Warbler and tripled my heart rate and all that! This was my first self-found Protho and my most wanted self-find (proportional to actual rarity) in the state and an absolutely electric experience. Photos.

Spotted by Liam at about 2:05pm.  It appeared over the cypresses to the north east, fairly high, and making a beeline to the North or NNE toward Marin.   It took me a few precious seconds to get on it - but when I did, it was obviously a pale falcon with long, tapered wings, and a pale face and underwing pattern, with some streaking on the neck and breast.   Caitlin called Prairie Falcon, and I called "dark armpits" characteristic to me of a juvie prairie.  Then we got a clearer view of the tail, which was sandy, pale colored like the rest of the body (eliminating MIKI in my mind).   Liam and Nancy got some diagnostic photos.  Awesome bird.
